defect.title: Three of the supervision TUI's five panes had no data source

defect.fix: Readiness and switches are filled from proctor_doctor. History is filled from proctor_history, which the first disposition wrongly recorded as unreachable. Two things were wrong with that reasoning. The verb exists: it is an internal socket verb the app's own History window already calls, kept out of ToolCatalogue so the shim, which gates tools/call on the catalogue, cannot route a model to it. And keeping it off the catalogue was never what made the trail unreadable to a model, because proctor_policy action audit is a catalogue tool that already opens the trail and hands back whole records. The projection this pane draws is strictly narrower than that one, so reading it here opens no path that was not already open and changes neither the sealing nor the gate. defect.title: The fix reached the CLI and the TUI and was filtered out of the window
defect.found: Re-photographing the status window after DEF-007 and counting three rows where four were expected
defect.detail:
StatusChecks classifies every grant name the health report can carry, and an unrecognised name falls to .tool — deliberately, because tool names are the half that grows. Input Monitoring was unrecognised, so the window's permissions filter removed it while the CLI and the TUI, which do not filter, both drew it.

The net that exists for exactly this did not fire. The drift test scans SessionDoctor.swift for `.init(name: "` and asserts set equality against the map, and the new grant was written as `.init(` then a newline then `name:` — so the scan never saw the name, both sets lacked it equally, and the assertion passed. Its only guard was against finding NOTHING, and it found plenty.
defect.fix: Input Monitoring is classified as a live-read permission. The scan is a whitespace-tolerant regular expression with a count floor, because a partial scan passes set equality against a map that is short by the same names.

defect.title: The suite carried an assertion that could not fail, and five tests it was not counting
defect.found: scripts/campaign/cannotfail_swift.py, written because warrant:assay's two scanners read TypeScript, JavaScript and Python and this suite is Swift
defect.detail: Across 103 files and 1,653 @Test functions the scan returned seven findings. One was a real hole: BuildInfoTests asserted `captured.builtAt == captured.builtAt`, a stored property compared to itself, in the test whose whole claim is that the captured value does not move when the file underneath it is replaced. It would have passed on a build where builtAt re-read the path on every access, which is the regression it is named after. Three more asserted only by not throwing, so they passed just as happily with the guard they are about deleted. Two were the scan's own false positives on a house style that asserts through a same-file helper. A sixth pattern was added after those: a defaulted read. `(try? read()) ?? ""` binds an input that could not be read to an empty one, and an assertion about what is ABSENT from an empty value passes for the wrong reason. Two in the suite, both in the audit trail's own tests, and both making the claim the trail exists to support: one asserted a redacted address is nowhere in the file, the other that a rotation leaves no backup or sidecar. Each passed just as happily when there was no file and no directory listing to look in.
defect.fix: The tautology now pins the value before the replacement and compares against that; armed by standing in what a re-reading implementation would report, and it bites. The three implicit tests say `#expect(throws: Never.self)`. The evidence writer, which asserted nothing at all, now reads its artifact back. The scan follows a same-file helper one level, which removes the false positives. Arming the scan found a defect in the scan: a one-line test body balances its braces on the signature line, so the line-based body finder skipped it and then consumed the next function's body looking for an opening brace. Rewritten to match braces by character, which raised the denominator from 1,648 @Test functions to 1,653 — five tests it had never been counting. Re-armed with four seeded defects across both shapes, all four caught, and clean on the real suite at 0 of 1,653. The two defaulted reads now read with `try`, so an unreadable trail fails the test rather than satisfying it, and each states positively that the thing it is about is there before asserting what is not. The pattern is a finding only where the defaulted value feeds a negated assertion inside the same test body, because a positive assertion on an empty value still fails. A seventh pattern counts rather than fails: a bare return above the first assertion. Three in the suite, all documented as conditional on a toolchain being present. Whether their guards hold on this machine is a separate question from whether they are honestly written, and it was settled by inverting each assertion and watching all three go red, so none of them returned early here.

defect.title: The live Maestro lane could not run on this machine, and its two tests fought over one simulator
defect.found: Running the opt-in live lane, which had not been run since 15 Aug, against a real simulator and a real Maestro
defect.detail: Two faults, and the product was right about the first one. The lane passed `device: nil` and relied on exactly one simulator being booted. Four are booted here, so the product refused, named all four and asked for one — correctly — and the whole live lane went red for a fact about the machine rather than about the code, which is the failure its opt-in switch exists to prevent. The second only appears when both tests run. They drive one simulator, and run concurrently they interleave on it: the determinism check scored its two repeats as divergent at command 4, a real divergence caused by the sibling test tapping the device mid-repeat. Alone the repeat test passed in 27s; as a suite it failed after 317s. A resource shared by two tests is a test-order dependency wearing a green tick.
defect.fix: The lane reads PROCTOR_LIVE_MAESTRO_DEVICE, falls back to the single booted simulator when there is exactly one, and otherwise does not run — naming a device on the operator's behalf would drive a simulator they may be using. The suite is `.serialized`. Measured 20 Aug 2026 against maestro 2.4.0 and a booted iPhone 16 Pro on iOS 18.2: both tests pass, 55.6s for the suite, green twice.

defect.title: TUISurface.Model's equality could not tell two models apart, and nothing noticed
defect.found: scripts/campaign/mutate_swift.py, written because warrant:assay's generator reads .ts .tsx .js .jsx .mjs .cjs .py and this package is Swift
defect.detail: 24 mutants over TUISurface, CLISurface, StatusChecks and RunHUDMenuBar: 14 killed, 10 survived, 0 unbuildable — a 41.7% survival rate. The survivors were not scattered. Every one of the ten was in TUISurface.Model's hand-written `==`. Flipping any `&&` there to `||` makes two models that differ in one field compare equal; flipping any field's `==` to `!=` makes two identical models compare unequal. Neither was noticed by 1,666 tests. The operator has no caller in the product today, which is why it survived and also why it was worth pinning: the obvious optimisation for the render loop is to skip a redraw when the model has not changed, and an `==` that cannot tell two models apart turns that into a screen that stops updating while a run is moving, which is the one failure this surface exists to prevent. It is hand-written, so a field added to Model and forgotten in `==` compiles, ships and is invisible.
defect.fix: TUIModelEqualityTests pins it three ways: two models built the same way are equal, a difference in any one of the thirteen fields makes them unequal, and every stored property Mirror can see has a variant in the list — a floor rather than a mirror of the operator, because reflection cannot see which fields a hand-written `==` reads, so a new field fails on the count before anybody has to notice it is missing from the comparison too. Re-measured with the same seed and the same targets, so it is the identical 24 mutants: 24 killed, 0 survived. 41.7% survival to 0%.

defect.title: Eight of the CLI's twenty-one verbs could not be given their main argument
defect.found: Checking a parked assumption in spec-PRO-0073.md against the code, rather than by anything failing
defect.detail: The spec recorded the step-batch fork and the assumption taken to unblock it: "support both, stdin JSON as the documented path". Neither half was built. Every flag value was typed as a string, a number or a bool, so `--steps '[…]'` reached the agent as a string and came back `proctor_act requires steps as an array`; and nothing in the CLI read stdin at all. Eight verbs declare an array or an object argument — act, zoom, wait, assert, flow, stability, computer and policy — so 8 of 21 could not be called for the thing they exist to do. `proctor act` in particular could not actuate anything.
defect.fix: CLIArguments in Core, so the decision is asserted against values written by hand rather than only reachable through a live agent. A flag value opening with [ or { is parsed as JSON and left as its string when it does not parse, because a caller who typed a selector should not be told their selector is malformed JSON. Arguments on stdin are merged underneath the flags, so a flag beside a pipe retargets a recorded batch instead of silently doing nothing. The first version inferred the stdin read from isatty and hung: any caller whose stdin is an open pipe nothing writes to — a CI runner, an agent harness — is not a terminal either, and `proctor doctor` waited forever on a read that never returned. Found by running it. It is now an explicit `-` or `--stdin`, which is the conventional idiom, cannot hang, and is still stdin as the documented path. Verified against a live wave-9 agent on all four paths: a JSON flag reached the agent as an array and got the tool's own answer; a piped batch performed a real foregrounded actuation; a flag beside a pipe won; and malformed stdin printed what was wrong and the remedy. The remedy string and the parser's token are pinned to each other by a test, because the first draft printed a remedy for a flag that did not exist.

defect.title: Half of ProctorCore's sampled mutants survived, and the second hand-written equality was one of them
defect.found: Widening the mutation assay from 4 files to all 77 of ProctorCore
defect.detail: 1,991 mutation sites over 77 files. 60 were selected by a recorded seed and 49 ran before the run was killed; 48 scored, 24 killed and 24 survived, 1 unbuildable. **50% survival**, which is in the range the literature would predict and is the first honest number this suite has had for anything wider than four files. 13 of the 24 survivors are integer literals, many of them geometry and layout constants in pure values. 11 are logic, and three were read closely: `RunHUDSurface.Chip.==` compared field counts and nothing had ever compared two chips with different counts — the second hand-written Equatable this wave has found unwatched, after TUISurface.Model, and the same shape both times because Swift cannot synthesise `==` over an array of tuples. The other two are equivalent mutants rather than gaps. `RunHUDGate.onSegment`'s `<=` boundary is unreachable: `onSegment` is only called from `crosses`, `crosses` only when no point is `contains`, and `contains` uses `>=`/`<=` on both axes, so every point that could exercise the boundary was caught one step earlier. `RunHistory`'s `a.offset < b.offset` sort tiebreak differs from `<=` only for equal offsets, and offsets are unique enumeration indices.
defect.fix: RunHUDChipEqualityTests pins field count, field name, field value and order, plus the empty chip. Armed against the exact mutant that survived — `count ==` to `count !=` — and it now fails five assertions. The two equivalent mutants are recorded rather than chased: a survivor no test could kill is not a gap, and a suite contorted to kill one is worse than the survivor. The remaining survivors are a named backlog with a number against them rather than an absence: 24 of 48 scored, of which 13 are integer literals and 8 are logic sites not yet read.

defect.title: The operator CLI exits 0 when a check fails, and its test passes because it invents the reply shape
defect.found: Phase 5 of the full campaign: writing the first case the cli lane has ever had, and running the real binary against the live agent
defect.detail:
CLISurface.exit(forReply:lane:) decides the process exit code. Its assertion branch reads `$0["ok"]?.boolValue == false` on each element of `assertions`. The product never puts an `ok` key on an assertion element: SessionAssert.swift:45 writes `"status": .string(result.status.rawValue)`, one of pass/fail/skipped. `nil == false` is false, so the predicate matches nothing and the function returns .ok. Neither the top-level `"ok": .bool(failed == 0 && skipped == 0)` at SessionAssert.swift:81 nor the top-level `"failed"` count at :77 is consulted at all.

MEASURED, twice, against the live agent from .build/debug/proctor-cli:
  proctor assert --window win:4:0 --assertions '[{"kind":"exists","identifier":"a-control-that-does-not-exist-xyzzy"}]'
    reply: {"ok":false,"passed":0,"failed":1,"assertions":[{"status":"fail",...}]}   exit=0, expected 1
  proctor wait --window win:4:0 --condition nodeExists --identifier a-control-that-does-not-exist-xyzzy --timeoutMs 1200
    reply: {"ok":false,"timedOut":true,...}                                            exit=0, expected 1

A third instance is present by inspection and not yet measured: proctor_kill emits a top-level `"failed"` count at SessionKill.swift:73 which nothing reads.

This defeats the stated purpose of the surface. spec-PRO-0073.md's exit table says '1 means the call worked and your check failed' and '1 and 3 must never be confused: one is a failed check, the other is nothing measured'. A CI job running `proctor assert` reads 0 and concludes the assertion passed while the JSON on its stdout says it failed.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: Tests/ProctorCoreTests/CLISurfaceTests.swift:175 'a failed assertion exits 1 — the call worked and the check did not' builds its own reply, `.object(["assertions": .array([.object(["ok": .bool(true)]), .object(["ok": .bool(false)])])])`, which is a shape the product does not emit. The test asserts a value the test itself wrote, so it passes against a fiction while the real path exits 0. Same shape as the A7 finding the PRO-0076 verifier caught: an assertion standing on a value constructed by the test rather than produced by the code under test.
defect.fixedBy: Sources/ProctorCore/CLISurface.swift:148-155 reads the top-level ok, the top-level failed count, and each assertion status == "fail"

defect.title: proctor_capture reports a fully transparent frame as status complete and trustworthy true
defect.found: PRO-0078 phase 6, building the REQ-004 effect witness: the first capture was taken of a Proctor-owned window, and the picture was read rather than trusted
defect.detail:
proctor_capture on win:1:0, CG window 121564, a window Proctor's own UI process owns, returned {"status":"complete","trustworthy":true,"dirtyRectCount":1,"dirtyArea":0,"width":1520,"height":1936,"scale":2}. Every one of the 2,942,720 pixels in the resulting PNG is RGBA(0,0,0,0). Measured by decompressing the IDAT stream and counting: alpha histogram is {0: 2942720}, and no pixel has a non-zero byte in any channel.

The emptiness itself is almost certainly correct behaviour. defect.title: Session.doctor blocks a cooperative thread inside SecStaticCodeCheckValidity, and fourteen such tests saturate the pool
defect.found: PRO-0083: the full suite stopped returning a verdict once nine integration tests were added beside it
defect.detail:
`Session.doctor` reaches `SignatureVerdictCache.verdict(for:)` for the cua-driver, which calls `CuaPreflight.verifySignature` and blocks in `SecStaticCodeCheckValidity` -> `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()`. It is a synchronous blocking call made from inside the session actor, so it occupies a Swift cooperative-pool thread for its whole duration, and that pool has exactly `activeProcessorCount` threads and never grows.

MEASURED 2026-08-21, by `sample` on the wedged process, repeatedly: fourteen to fifteen of the sixteen cooperative threads inside that one call, in `BrowserLaneWiringTests`, `ObscuraPresenceWiringTests`, `ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests`, `GuestDoctorWiringTests`, `MachineDisclosureWiringTests`, `DoctorReplyWiringTests` and `ToolchainOnThisMachineTests`. The same thread ids in the same frames across samples seven minutes apart, with 3.4 seconds of CPU consumed in twelve minutes of elapsed time. Meanwhile `codesign -v` on the same binary returned instantly from a shell, so the system was not the bottleneck.

WHAT THAT MAKES FRAGILE. With the pool at fourteen of sixteen there are two slots left, and anything that needs a third while holding a lock other tests block on deadlocks the whole run. `TrailIsolation` is exactly such a lock: every trail suite takes it from a cooperative thread. PRO-0083's witnesses hit this three separate ways and each is now avoided in the test rather than in the product — blocking work moved onto owned threads, the trail held only across code that never suspends, and the witness sessions given probes that answer from a table instead of from this machine. Before those, the suite ran to a verdict in 12 to 26 seconds with these files skipped and never returned with them present.

NOT FIXED HERE, and it is a product-shaped question rather than a test one: whether a health report should do a blocking code-signature check on the actor at all, or hand it to a detached executor and report `unconfirmed` until it answers. The same shape is already recorded once as DEF-029, where the wall clock rather than the pool was what moved. Recorded because a suite that deadlocks under load deadlocks in CI, where load is normal.

RE-MEASURED ON THE RESUME, 2026-08-21: still live, and the mechanism narrowed a step further - see DEF-044. The blocked frame is `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()`, so the cooperative thread is not merely slow inside a syscall, it is waiting on libdispatch global-pool workers that this suite's child processes compete for. The three test-side mitigations recorded above reduce this item's contribution but cannot remove it: the concurrency that saturates the pool is the wiring suites' own.

defect.title: SignatureVerdictCache verifies outside its own lock, so N cold caches verify one file N times at once
defect.found: PRO-0083 resume: the full suite failed deterministically at 143s with two bound overruns, and wedged entirely at higher load
defect.detail:
`SignatureVerdictCache.verdict(for:)` takes its lock, misses, RELEASES the lock, and only then calls `verify(path)`. Concurrent callers with a cold cache therefore all enter `SecStaticCodeCheckValidity` together rather than one doing the work and the rest waiting on it. There is no single-flight, and the doc comment above the method - "verifying only when the file is one this cache has not already seen" - describes behaviour the method does not have under concurrency.

MEASURED 2026-08-21 by `sample`, twice, on two separate full runs: fifteen of the sixteen cooperative threads inside `SecStaticCodeCheckValidityWithErrors` -> `SecStaticCode::staticValidate` -> `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()` -> `_dispatch_group_wait_slow` -> `__ulock_wait`, in ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests, ObscuraPresenceWiringTests, ToolchainDoctorTests and GuestProviderTests. `staticValidate` farms its page hashing to the libdispatch global pool and waits on a group, so a blocked cooperative thread is waiting on a worker pool that any second load can starve.

WHY A PER-INSTANCE FIX DOES NOT CLOSE IT: each Session holds its own cache, so the fifteen concurrent verifications are fifteen SEPARATE cache instances each legitimately missing once. Single-flighting one instance would not deduplicate them; the dedupe would have to be process-wide, which is a design change rather than a lock move. Recorded rather than fixed for that reason.

ATTRIBUTION, measured rather than assumed: the full suite WITHOUT this item's two suites passes 1,818 tests in 6.5 seconds with ScreenRecordingProbeWiringTests' bounded test taking 0.655s. This item's two suites alone pass in 9.5 seconds. Together the run takes 143 seconds and that same bounded test overruns its 5-second bound to 10.6s. The suites do not fail each other's assertions; they exhaust a shared pool.

INTERMITTENT AFTER THIS ITEM'S FIX, and measured as such. Removing the forging arm's launch took the full run from 143s to 16.4s and from four issues to one, and it went green at 1,827 tests in 21.376s. It does not go green every time: sampled during a later wedge, fifteen threads sat in the same staticValidate stack and NONE of them were this item's - `pro83.`-named threads in the sample: zero, ExternalWitnessTests frames: zero. This suite's child processes perturb the libdispatch global pool and the pre-existing race is then lost by the wiring suites on their own. Run tally on the fixed tree: with this item's suites present, 2 green of 4 (21.376s and 20.261s green, one failing only on the neighbouring 5-second bound at 16.4s, one wedged); with them skipped, 2 of 2. Two skip runs is not proof the wedge cannot happen without this item, and it is not claimed as one.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT, neither of them this item's to do: a process-wide dedupe of signature verification in `Sources/`, or replacing Foundation `Process` with raw posix_spawn/waitpid in these tests so no child registers a dispatch source on the global queue that `Security::Dispatch::Group::wait()` is starving for.
defect.evidence: Recorded again as DEF-050, which is `fixed`. Sources/ProctorAgent/Session/SignatureVerdictCache.swift:149-171 — a caller that finds `waiting[identity]` populated appends its continuation and returns rather than entering the verification, so N cold callers on one identity cost one verification.
defect.fix: SignatureVerdictCache.shared is the ToolProbes default, keyed by FileIdentity with a 16-entry bound, and single-flight through the `waiting` map.

defect.title: policy.json is written world-readable while every audit file in the same subsystem is opened 0600
defect.found: PRO-0089, reading the two stores side by side in PolicyStore.swift
defect.detail:
`PolicyStore.save` creates its directory with `.posixPermissions: 0o700` and then writes the file with `Data.write(to:options:.atomic)`, which takes the umask default. Measured on this Mac: `-rw-r--r-- policy.json` inside `drwx------ policy/`. `AuditLog` in the same file opens `audit.jsonl`, `audit.lock` and `audit.pub` with an explicit `0o600` and sets `0o600` on its temporaries; measured `-rw------- audit.jsonl`.

The 0700 directory is what carries the protection, so this is an inconsistency rather than an exposure: another user cannot traverse the directory to reach the file. It matters if the file is ever copied, archived, or the directory's mode is relaxed.

NOT FIXED HERE, deliberately. This item is about test seams; changing the on-disk mode of an operator's existing configuration file is a separate change with its own migration question (an existing 0644 file keeps its mode through an atomic replace on some paths and not others), and fixing it in passing would put an unrelated line in this diff.
defect.fix: PolicyStore.save no longer uses Data.write(to:options:.atomic), which takes no mode and so took the umask default. It opens its own temporary in the policy directory with Darwin.open(O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_TRUNC, 0o600) — the same explicit open AuditLog uses for audit.jsonl, audit.lock and audit.pub — writes it, fsyncs, closes, and replaces atomically with FileManager.replaceItemAt(options: [.usingNewMetadataOnly]). The mode is set at creation rather than by a chmod afterwards, because a file that existed world-readable for an instant has been world-readable. O_EXCL is what binds the mode argument: open applies it only when it creates the file, so O_TRUNC over a stale 0644 temporary would reuse that mode. .usingNewMetadataOnly is what narrows an operator's existing 0644 file, which replaceItemAt would otherwise carry across forever. The temporary is uniquely named per call: O_EXCL on one fixed name would refuse a concurrent save that Data.write(options: .atomic) allowed through, and two sessions in one agent share operatorDirectory. CASE-0198 guards that.

defect.title: The signature verdict cache was scoped per Session while the verdict it holds is a fact about a file, so fifteen sessions verified one 82 MB binary at once and starved the cooperative pool
defect.found: Raised by PRO-0083's verifier as DEF-044; reproduced and closed by PRO-0087
defect.detail: SignatureVerdictCache deduplicates a 0.32-0.39s SecStaticCodeCheckValidity per instance, and ToolProbes.init default-constructed one per probe set, which is one per Session. The file's own header argued that two concurrent callers both verifying was 'wasted work and nothing else' and that single-flight 'would buy one saved hash and a state machine to get wrong'; both halves assumed there were two callers, and the scoping made fifteen. Server.dispatchBlocking then had no thread for its Task.detached, and a peer with a 10s SO_RCVTIMEO went unserved, which took REQ-035's forged-caller witness with it.
defect.evidence: docs/test-campaign/evidence/PRO-0087/wedge-before.txt and wedge-before-2.txt, two samples of one hung run five minutes apart, each showing 15 of 22 threads inside SecStaticCodeCheckValidity on com.apple.root.default-qos.cooperative and blocked in Security::Dispatch::Group::wait() for the whole five-second sample; wedge-after-blocking.txt, the same measurement against the blocking fix, showing the wedge reshaped rather than removed. Run counts in docs/test-campaign/evidence/PRO-0087/run-ledger.md.
defect.fix: SignatureVerdictCache.shared is the ToolProbes default; the store is keyed by FileIdentity with a 16-entry bound; and verdict(for:) is async, so callers arriving on an identity already being verified register a continuation and give their thread back while one verification runs on a Thread of its own, off the cooperative pool. defect.title: A quoted placeholder id is read as a citation at confidence 1.0
defect.note:
reckon's ID_RE scans a brief's whole body for id-shaped tokens with no code-fence and no placeholder exclusion, so a quoted example id becomes a citation at confidence 1.0. PRO-0102's verifier built a brief whose only id-shaped token was CASE-9999 inside an example command; it classed unbuilt and product-work, on the reasoning that the registry holds none of the ids it cites. That is DEF-214's shape one hop out — a token that is not a citation, labelled cited at full confidence — and it routes a brief to the one class PRO-0102 narrowed unbuilt down to. It fires 0 times across the 91 real briefs in this repo, so it is latent rather than active, and the repair is one predicate in build_join plus a fixture. Gemini raised it independently in the same verification. Found by the non-AC findings sweep at PRO-0102's verification.

THE ZERO IS A FACT ABOUT THIS REPO'S IDIOM RATHER THAN ABOUT THE RISK, and a sibling project is concretely exposed. Its briefs carry ids in prose and in fenced command blocks, and its citation convention is that a brief names the defects it closes — so a brief discussing a neighbouring defect is textually identical to one that owns it. A repository citing by convention has the opposite prior to this one, where all 24 legacy citations happen to sit in real prose at fence depth 0. Recording '0 occurrences across 91 briefs' without that caveat would invite the next reader to treat the defect as theoretical.

defect.title: An unrecognised status word decides the headline, and it can fail in either direction
defect.note:
reckon classifies a defect as broken and as remaining work on any status word other than `fixed`. This registry uses only `fixed` and `open`, so the behaviour is correct here and PRO-0102's acceptance is unaffected; it is recorded because 1.1.0 has been announced to nine projects as the version to run.

MEASURED IN A SIBLING PROJECT the same evening, not predicted: its register reads fixed 55, open 11, partially-fixed 3, characterised 2, resolved 1, not-a-defect 1, inconclusive 1, vacuous 1. Six rows land in broken and count as work owed against an adjudicated true queue of nine briefs — a large proportional error on a small true number, which is the shape that gets believed. Fifteen where nine is the truth reads as a backlog rather than as a bug.

THE WORD LIST WAS WRONG WHEN FIRST FILED, corrected by the project that owns those rows. `by design`, `invalid`, `obsolete`, `superseded`, `cannot reproduce`, `resolved`, `not-a-defect` and `vacuous` do not owe remaining work. `partially-fixed` DOES, and was wrongly grouped with them here: a half still broken owes a reproduction for that half, and none of that project's three partially-fixed rows had one. Retiring it would make the tool under-report for the first time.

AND THE REAL FINDING IS LARGER THAN THE LIST, which is why this row is titled for the mechanism rather than for the six words. An unrecognised vocabulary item fails in TWO directions and only one of them is visible. reckon over-reports on an unknown word: annoying, self-announcing, and it makes somebody look. The same project checked its own reproduction gate for this shape and found the opposite failure — it selected its population with a single status string, `open`, so a register growing a word meaning still-broken (`regressed`, `reopened`) would have dropped those rows out of the obligation entirely while the gate went on printing a clean count over a quietly smaller population. A clean green is a worse failure than an inflated backlog, because nothing about it asks to be checked.

SO THE REPAIR IS NOT A LONGER LIST. Classify every status as owing or not owing, and make an unclassified word A FINDING THAT NAMES THE WORD AND ITS ROW COUNT rather than a default in either direction. Widening its own gate that way immediately surfaced five real defects there and took owing from 19 to 24. Same shape as DEF-201 and DEF-203: an input a check cannot classify should be a finding, not a silent pass or a silent fail.

defect.title: The installed reckon plugin is still 1.0.0, and 1.0.0 crashes on this registry
defect.found: PRO-0103, while resolving which copy of the tool a wave-close reading should run
defect.detail: ~/.claude/plugins/cache/fledgeling-plugins/reckon/ holds one directory, 1.0.0, whose plugin.json declares 1.0.0 and whose reckon.py contains zero occurrences of 'unjoined'. The shared source at ~/Dev/fledgeling-plugins/plugins/reckon declares 1.1.0. Running the cached copy against docs/test-campaign exits 1 with AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'lower' at tokens(), because this registry carries a case's evidence as a list of paths. So somebody following reckon's own SKILL.md, which resolves its scripts from the installed skill directory, gets a crash rather than a reading, and the version announced to nine projects as the one to run is not the version installed here.
defect.note: The crash is the lucky half. A registry without list-valued evidence would get a silent 1.0.0 reading instead, with fixed defects classed broken and unjoined briefs classed unbuilt, which is exactly the headline the first reckoning here had to decline. Recorded as low severity because the shared source is correct and the cache refreshes on the next marketplace sync, and because scripts/reckoning/reckoning.py now reads the manifest version and the class list before it measures anything, so this repository's own cadence refuses the stale copy rather than believing it. CASE-0447.

defect.title: Two different tools with the same version string compare as the same tool
defect.note: reckoning.py's compare refuses a tool on disk that is not the one that took the current reading, and the refusal is keyed on a declared version string rather than on the tool. PRO-0103's verifier proved the gap two ways. The 1.0.0 cache relabelled 1.1.0 is caught, but by the class-vocabulary check (missing `unjoined`) rather than by the version. And the real 1.1.0 source, with CLASSES and ratchet intact and classify() altered to reclassify unjoined as verified-done, manifest reading 1.1.0, was ACCEPTED at exit 0 — and the published delta silently became -163 tool / +79 project against a true -88 / +4. run.json already records tool.source_commit; compare never reads it. This is the same shape as DEF-216 one level up: a version string is exactly what goes wrong, so a version string cannot be the test. The repair is to compare the artifact rather than its label.

defect.title: cmd_take discards the digests sweep() computed, so the witness records names without content
defect.note: sweep() walks the run directory and computes a byte count and sha256 for every file; cmd_take stores only the filenames and the count. So the effect witness for REQ-102 can say two files appeared and cannot say what was in them, and a file replaced between the two sweeps would be invisible. It also let CASE-0456 record a claim nobody could check: the case said four files each with byte count and sha256, run.json holds two names and no digests, and campaign.py counted the case witnessed without opening the artifact. The case is corrected; this row is the instrument. Two repairs, and the second is the one that generalises: store what sweep() already computed, and have the witness check read the artifact rather than the case's description of it.

defect.title: resolve_tree prints a path that does not exist in its own refusal
defect.note: git() strips its output, so a porcelain status line arrives as `M docs/...` rather than ` M docs/...`, and the [3:] slice that was written to drop the two status characters and the space removes the first character of the path instead: `docs/test-campaign/cases.json` is refused as `ocs/test-campaign/cases.json`. Untracked entries are unaffected because `?? ` survives the strip intact. The refusal is correct and its message names a file nobody can find, which sends the reader looking for a phantom; and with --allow-dirty the mangled name is written into run.json.dirty_inputs, where it becomes a permanent record of a path that never existed. It fires on the commonest case, a modified tracked file.

defect.title: Four ledger rows have no spec file, so two briefs have no artifact that could cite them
defect.found: PRO-0101 provenance sweep, 2026-08-22
defect.detail: docs/feature-specs/LEDGER.md carries 103 ids against 99 files in docs/specs. The four with no spec are PRO-0022 (A drawing fault must not kill the agent, Merged 2026-08-14), PRO-0031 (The health report is complete, Retired), PRO-0039 (Page-scoped refusal, Retired) and PRO-0092 (ProctorAgent's mutants mostly survive, Ready for AI). Two of them are why the reverse direction cannot close by citation alone: docs/features-to-triage/23-drawing-fault-must-not-kill-the-agent.md is PRO-0022 and 40-page-scoped-refusal.md is PRO-0039 — each brief's own banner names its id — and neither has a spec to carry a **Brief:** line. No spec lacks a ledger row, so the gap is one-directional.
defect.fix: NOT FIXED HERE. A spec citation needs a spec, and writing three retrospective specs for two retired items and one merged item is a different piece of work with its own decision about whether a retired item earns a spec at all. Recorded instead in docs/feature-specs/UNCLAIMED-BRIEFS.md, which is read by spec_citation_measure.py, so briefs 23 and 40 are accounted for with their reason rather than counted as unclaimed. PRO-0092 closes its own row when its spec is written at plan time.

defect.title: Three citation checks accept inputs their names imply they reject
defect.note: Three checks in spec_citation_measure.py accept inputs their names imply they reject, each found by building the evasion against a scratch copy at PRO-0101's verification. (1) `every spec carries a parseable citation` passes when the only brief path sits in a fenced code block, an HTML comment or a struck-through line, because the legacy fallback is a bare BODY_PATH.search over the whole text; a **Brief:** header inside a fence in the first 20 lines counts too. (2) `every none citation names its origin` passes on `none. See docs/nowhere/imaginary-source.md` and on any backtick pair padded to 20 characters — the floor makes a citation name something, not resolve to it. (3) `every brief is claimed or registered` is satisfied by an incidental mention in an unrelated spec, so a brief nobody built from reads as claimed. None of the three is dead: each is armed and bites on the case it was written for, and the delivered tree exploits none of them because all 24 legacy citations are real prose at fence depth 0. SAME CLASS AS DEF-201 IN A DIFFERENT INSTRUMENT: a scanner reading a whole document for a token, with no exclusion for fences, comments or struck-through text, cannot tell a citation from a mention of one. Two tools in two repositories grew the same blind spot independently, which makes it a shape to check for rather than a bug either author made. The repair is not a longer floor: an input a check cannot classify should be a finding that names it, not a pass or a fail by default.

defect.title: Three boolean arguments are published with no stated default while the decoder has one
defect.found: PRO-0092, building the schema-versus-decoder agreement check for survivors 2 and 8
defect.detail: 28 boolean properties across the 21 tools in ToolCatalogue. 25 state their default in their own description; 3 did not — proctor_stability.includeTiles, proctor_capture.tileHashes and proctor_doctor.verbose. Each has a default in Dispatch.swift, false in all three cases, so a caller omitting the argument gets a behaviour the published schema does not describe. Found by the check going looking for stability.includeTiles and finding nothing to compare against, which is the failure mode of a two-source check whose second source is silent: it passes by comparing nothing.
defect.note: FIXED. The three descriptions now state their defaults, which is a documentation repair with its own value and is also what lets REQ-108's check reach survivor 2 of PRO-0080's sample. The decoder was not changed; the schema was the half that was silent.

defect.title: mutate_swift.py splices by byte offset and never reads back
defect.note: apply() writes the mutation by byte offset and does not re-read the file, so it cannot report that the substitution happened. Its sibling instrument does: mutation_seam_arm.py asserts an occurrence count of 1, then re-reads and requires the `after` text present and the `before` text gone. The runner cannot go INERT the way an anchor-string mutator can, because it splices unconditionally — its failure mode is worse in kind, because a wrong-offset write would be silent and would grade pristine or wrongly-edited code as a survivor. PRO-0092's verification reconstructed all 24 mutants against the tree the run used (6b3721c) and confirmed each recorded offset holds the recorded `before` text and that a simulated splice changes exactly one line at exactly the recorded line number, so all 20 survivors and all 4 kills in THIS sample demonstrably landed. That is a reconstruction by a verifier, not a proof by the instrument, and the distinction is the defect: the next sample gets no such reconstruction unless somebody does it by hand. Port the read-back. A survivor has two readings — the guard is decorative, or the mutation never happened — and only the instrument can tell them apart at the moment it matters.

defect.title: mutation_seam_arm.py scores any non-zero exit as armed, including a process that died
defect.note: The arm records `armed = code != 0`, so a run that aborts on a signal counts as red. CASE-0461's mutant kills by trapping: signal 5, zero verdict lines, and the suite's own `FAIL: no swift-testing verdict line`. That case is correct — its log proves the named test was running when the process trapped — but the rule that scored it cannot distinguish a test that failed from a process that died in setup, and the second is the shape that has already cost this campaign a false arming. The repair is the same predicate the suite already applies to itself: an arming owes a verdict line naming the test that failed, and an exit with no verdict line is `inconclusive` rather than armed.

defect.title: Thirty-five images in the shots directory that nothing publishes and no manifest names
defect.note:
capture-lineage.py --gate exits 2 on main: `published captures: 8 · distinct images: 8 · files in shots dir: 43`, with 35 UNACCOUNTED images — a file in the shots directory that no subject publishes and no manifest entry names. The tool's remedy is publish it, delete it, or record an `unpublishedReason` on its captures.json entry.

THIS IS TOOL MOVEMENT REVEALING A PRE-EXISTING CONDITION, NOT A REGRESSION, and it was established by holding the tool constant across three trees rather than argued: the current capture-lineage gives the identical reading — exit 2, judged 6 of 8, ratchet 6, 35 hard failures — at dd1a443 (now), at eed148f (wave-16 close) and at 3d6fb15 (the wave-15 merge, before any of tonight's work). ORCHESTRATOR.md records this gate at exit 0 with judged 6 of 8 and ratchet 6 held, which was true of the version that ran it. test-campaign moved to 0.9.6 mid-session and the gate got stricter. The ratchet still holds at 6, so nothing has got worse by the tool's own measure.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING TIDINESS: the gate's own words are that every finding it makes is derived from published captures, so a file nobody publishes is a capture the gate cannot see — and it cites a campaign that read `published captures: 0 · files in shots dir: 11` and exited 0. Thirty-five unpublished images are thirty-five pictures a reader will take as evidence and the instrument cannot speak for. Most carry surface-shaped names (surf-001 through surf-016) from earlier waves, so they are probably real captures that were taken and never published, which is the recoverable case.

DELETION IS NOT THE DEFAULT REMEDY HERE even though the tool offers it: each image needs a per-file disposition, and discarding evidence to clear a gate is the move this campaign refuses. Found by auditing every gate's exit code and denominator across main and a clean `worktree add --detach` tree, prompted by a sibling project finding a step that exited 0 on its own machine and 1 on a clean tree 

CLOSED BY PRO-0107, and by accounting rather than by shrinking: 43 files before and 43 after, 8 published before and 8 after, 0 deleted. Each of the 35 was opened and looked at, and each carries an `unpublishedReason` on its captures.json entry naming what the picture shows. `capture-lineage.py docs/test-campaign --gate` exits 0 with `COUNTED APART (35) — admissible, not judged`, judged 6 of 8, ratchet 6 held. The gate was watched to fail first: removing one `unpublishedReason` returned exit 2 with that file named, and restoring it reproduced the passing reading byte for byte. What the reading found is in DEF-218 through DEF-223 — nine app-icon renders under engine-surface names, three frames with no image in them, one image under three captions across two sweeps, and a file named agent-down showing a Ready window. The brief's assumption that the surface-shaped names meant real captures from earlier waves was wrong for nine of them, which is the more valuable half of the answer.

defect.title: Nine files named for nine engine surfaces are app-icon renders (recorded)
defect.note:
surf-001-mcp-stdio, surf-002-tool-catalogue, surf-003-process-directed, surf-011-stability, surf-012-audit-policy, surf-013-guest-provider, surf-014-ios-maestro, surf-015-reflector and surf-016-install-notarize are every one of them a Proctor app-icon render — the dark window dissolving into orange squares, 1024x1024, on the icon corpus's warm ground. Not one is a picture of the engine its filename names.

THE MECHANISM IS A SCRIPT, NOT A MISFILING: scripts/build_test_campaign.py lines 282-296 copy design/icon/audit-renders/* and design/icon/runs/*/candidate-1024.png into evidence/shots/ under surface-shaped destination names, so a filename claiming SURF-001 was manufactured by a copy statement. surf-016-install-notarize.png is byte-identical to design/icon/icon-proctor-1024.png (sha256 a67cf67af07e…), which settles the mechanism rather than inferring it. Four other destinations in that same list — surf-006, surf-007, surf-008-status-window and surf-009-walkthrough — were later replaced by real window captures with manifests written at the shutter, which is why they are published and these nine are not.

RECORDED RATHER THAN FIXED: the repair is either a real capture per engine surface through capture_with_manifest.py or the removal of the copy list from build_test_campaign.py, and neither is PRO-0107's scope. Each of the nine now carries an `unpublishedReason` saying what the picture actually is, so a reader is told rather than left to read the name. Found by opening all 35 unaccounted files, which is the only way it is findable.

defect.title: Three files named for the takeover shield contain no image at all (recorded)
defect.note:
surf-005-takeover-sck-external.png, surf-005-takeover-sck-laptop.png and surf-005-takeover-sck-window.png are entirely transparent: 0 non-transparent pixels of 14,745,600, 7,720,704 and 677,888 respectively, and exactly 1 distinct RGBA value each, measured off the files with Pillow.

evidence/hud-capture-channels.json already lists all three under `framesThatWereNotEvidence` and keeps them as the record of the false raster pass this campaign corrected — SCFrameStatus `complete` over a frame with nothing in it, the same instrument fault CASE-0059 carries. So the files are deliberately kept and the record for them is right; what was wrong is that three names claiming the takeover shield sat in the gallery with nothing declaring them. Now declared. RECORDED rather than fixed because the underlying fault is the capture channel's, not this directory's.

defect.title: sweepK-scaling.json lists two frames its own mode table has no capture of (recorded)
defect.note:
evidence/sweepK-scaling.json names four files in its `shots` array and records four modes whose capture sizes are 970x773, 820x654, 970x773 and 781x961. sweepK-scale-small.png is 970x773 and sweepK-scale-1x.png is 820x654, so two of the four tie. sweepK-external.png and sweepK-laptop.png are both 900x833, which matches no mode in the table, and no file in the directory is 781x961, so the sweep's own baseline frame is absent while two frames it lists came from outside its measurements.

Both pictures are the status window with letter-spaced capital section headers — the pre-sentence-case build, an earlier wave than the published SURF-008 frame — so they are real captures of a real surface rather than debris. RECORDED: what the sweep measured is unaffected (examined=4 failures=0 stands on the mode table, not on the files), and the finding is that a `shots` list is not tied to the measurements beside it.

defect.title: One image carries three captions across two unrelated sweeps, and two wedged timestamps share one frame (recorded)
defect.note:
sweepK-theme-before.png, sweepL-wedged-t1.png and sweepL-wedged-recovered.png are byte-identical (sha256 670a93988315…), and the picture is a dark Ready status window. So sweep K's dark theme baseline, sweep L's earliest wedged frame and sweep L's recovery frame are one file under three captions, across two sweeps that share no measurement.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, ONE OF THEM WORSE THAN THE OTHER. A Ready window at t+1 is defensible on its own terms, because the window's timeout is 5s and at t+1 it has nothing to report yet. The recovery frame is not: evidence/sweepL-halfopen.json records recoveredAfterSIGCONT true, and a recovery shown by the same bytes as the pre-recovery frame witnesses no transition.

AND THE SAME SHAPE ONE STEP LATER: sweepL-wedged-t7.png and sweepL-wedged-t14.png are byte-identical to each other (5c7d4535e70c…), both showing `Agent down — the Proctor agent did not answer within 5s`, so the wedge is witnessed once rather than at two times. RECORDED rather than fixed: the sweeps' verdicts rest on their JSON records and their timings, not on the frames, and re-running them is not this item's scope.

defect.title: sweepL-status-agent-down.png depicts a Ready window, and the two agent-down frames are one image (recorded)
defect.note:
The sharpest name-versus-content mismatch in the directory. sweepL-status-agent-down.png shows a green Ready pill, Accessibility and Screen Recording both Granted, and `Ready. Every permission Proctor needs is granted.` — no agent-down state anywhere in the frame.

Its own record explains the picture while the filename inverts it: evidence/sweeps-kl.json says `Agent down at t+0.71s and t+3.63s after bootout+SIGKILL … The earlier Ready frame was captured inside one 2s doctor tick. DEF-002 retracted.` So this file is that earlier Ready frame, and the frames that do show `Agent down` are sweepL-status-t0.6.png and sweepL-status-t3.5.png — which are byte-identical to each other (4f8c11912bbd…), so the two sampled times are one picture and the second is not independently witnessed.

RECORDED: renaming an evidence file changes what every existing citation of it resolves to, and the honest cheap repair is the declaration, which is done. A reader following the filename would have concluded the opposite of what the sweep found.

defect.title: A file's surface prefix binds it to a surface the picture does not show (recorded)
defect.note:
Two instances, both found by opening the file. surf-004-drawn-pointer.png is prefixed for SURF-004, the Run HUD, and shows no HUD: it is the drawn pointer glyph alone on an otherwise empty 3456x2234 frame, 3,739 non-transparent pixels of 7,720,704 and 173 distinct RGBA — the pointer belongs to SURF-003's actuation overlay. surf-008-about.png is prefixed for SURF-008, the Status & Diagnostics Window, and is the About Proctor panel: app icon, `Proctor`, `Version 0.1.0 (1)`, `Proctor is released under the MIT licence.` at 704x518. No surface in this inventory is the About panel, so there is no subject it could be published under.

Both are real pictures of real Proctor surfaces, which is why neither was deleted. RECORDED: the repair for the first is a re-capture under SURF-003 with a manifest, and for the second an inventory surface for the About panel; both are new work rather than PRO-0107's.

defect.title: Case evidence and the lineage manifest disagree about the same five files (recorded)
defect.note:
capture-lineage reads only the `shot` field on surfaces and flow steps. cases.json cites shots directly in `evidence`, and the two registries now disagree about five files.

THREE RASTER-VISUAL PASSES STAND ON CAPTURES THE MANIFEST DECLARES UNPUBLISHED: CASE-0008 → surf-004-run-hud.png, CASE-0010 → surf-005-takeover-shield.png, CASE-0011 → surf-008-tools.png. Stated precisely, because the halves differ: each of the three DOES carry a case-level `capture.method` (`screencapture -l on the panel window number, exclusion lifted by PROCTOR_OVERLAY_CAPTURE` twice, `ScreenCaptureKit window-scoped` once), so the channel is named. What none of them has is a captures.json row with a target recorded at the shutter, which is what publishing requires and what PRO-0107 declined to write after the fact. So a reader of the evidence page sees three passing pixel claims whose pictures the lineage record says nothing speaks for.

TWO OUTCOME PASSES CITE FRAMES THIS ITEM SHOWED MISNAMED OR DUPLICATED: CASE-0028 cites sweepL-status-agent-down.png, which depicts a Ready window (DEF-222), together with the byte-identical t0.6 and t3.5 pair; CASE-0029 cites sweepL-wedged-recovered.png, which is byte-identical to the earliest wedged frame (DEF-221). Both cases' verdicts rest on their sweep JSON rather than on the frames, so neither verdict is wrong — the frames beside them are.

Found by an out-of-family review of PRO-0107 (gemini-3.7-flash-high) and confirmed against cases.json rather than taken on the review's word. RECORDED: the repair is a re-capture through capture_with_manifest.py for the three, and a re-run for the two, both new work.

defect.title: A passing case cites a shots file that does not exist, and no gate looks (recorded)
defect.note:
CASE-0100 is an effect-witness pass whose evidence names `evidence/shots/a3-walkthrough-permissions-disabled.png`, and no such file exists in the shots directory — the file that does exist is step-a3-walkthrough-primary-disabled.png, published under STEP-A3-PRIMARY-DISABLED and cited by CASE-0106.

WHY EVERY GATE PASSES OVER IT. campaign.py checks that a pass names at least one evidence artifact and never that the artifact exists, except on the raster rungs, where `inspect_raster` resolves the path and reports `no file at that path` — which is exactly how CASE-0318's three missing files became a standing blocker. CASE-0100 stands at effect-witness, so its path is never resolved. capture-lineage never reads cases.json at all. So a dangling picture link on a passing case is invisible to both instruments that could see it, and visible to a reader who clicks it.

RECORDED: the fix is one line in cases.json if the intended file is the step-a3 capture, and a re-capture if it is not, and establishing which is not something this item can do from the filename — which is the whole lesson of PRO-0107. Found while confirming DEF-224.
